context.concept_name: Handle AWS automation errors with bounded retries and useful reporting; AWS SDK call is a supplied ready function, not an assumed skill or prerequisite

coverage.learning_objective: Handle AWS automation errors with bounded retries

required_facts.statement: AWS SDK retries cover selected transient or throttling errors rather than making every failed request safe to repeat.

Set botocore.config.Config(retries={"mode": "standard", "total_max_attempts": APPROVED_ATTEMPTS}) on the supplied Boto3 client to bound requests with the SDK’s backoff; do not wrap terminal errors in an unbounded retry loop.

Catch botocore.exceptions.ClientError around the supplied call, inspect its response["Error"]["Code"] and response["Error"]["Message"] and preserve response["ResponseMetadata"]["RequestId"] when present; report the terminal failure or exhausted retry outcome.
When configuring Boto3, total_max_attempts includes the initial request, whereas max_attempts in a Config object counts retries after the initial request.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied AWS automation call encounters an error. The program needs a finite retry budget for eligible errors and useful terminal reporting, not an unbounded loop that repeats every failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: AWS SDK retries cover selected transient or throttling errors rather than making every failed request safe to repeat.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set botocore.config.Config(retries={"mode": "standard", "total_max_attempts": APPROVED_ATTEMPTS}) on the supplied Boto3 client to bound requests with the SDK’s backoff; do not wrap terminal errors in an unbounded retry loop.

Catch botocore.exceptions.ClientError around the supplied call, inspect its response["Error"]["Code"] and response["Error"]["Message"] and preserve response["ResponseMetadata"]["RequestId"] when present; report the terminal failure or exhausted retry outcome.

When configuring Boto3, total_max_attempts includes the initial request, whereas max_attempts in a Config object counts retries after the initial request.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set the supplied Boto3 client's Config retries to standard mode with total_max_attempts set to the approved finite attempt budget. If the example budget is 3, that includes the initial request and leaves at most two retries. In a Config object, max_attempts instead counts retries after the initial request; using 3 there describes a different budget. Around the supplied call, catch ClientError and inspect Error Code and Message. Preserve ResponseMetadata RequestId when present in the response. Report terminal failure or exhausted retries with that evidence. The SDK retries selected transient or throttling errors with its backoff; this example does not declare every failed request safe to repeat or add a separate unlimited wrapper.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: total_max_attempts and Config max_attempts do not count the same thing. The former includes the first request; the latter counts retries after it. Also, retry support covers selected errors, so a terminal failure must be reported rather than retried indefinitely.

video_need.reason: Initial-request versus retry counting and terminal exception reporting benefit from an annotated bounded-call execution trace.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure the supplied Boto3 client with standard SDK retries and the approved total attempt budget. Add ClientError handling around the supplied ready AWS-call function and report the final outcome without implementing the AWS operation or adding an independent retry loop.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied client uses standard mode and total_max_attempts equal to APPROVED_ATTEMPTS. The supplied call is invoked once at the application level. Terminal or exhausted-retry ClientError outcomes retain Error Code, Error Message, and RequestId when present, and are reported rather than repeated indefinitely.

live_code.required_skill: Apply a bounded SDK retry configuration and catch ClientError around a supplied function, extracting error evidence for final reporting.
allowed_syntax: Dictionary literals with string keys and an approved integer attempt budget
Calling supplied client-setup, ready-call, and outcome-reporting functions
try / except ClientError as error / else
Dictionary .get() for optional ResponseMetadata and RequestId
blocked_syntax: while loops around the supplied call
for loops that repeat the supplied call
Direct AWS service-operation calls replacing the supplied ready function
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide APPROVED_ATTEMPTS with the example value 3, a supplied Boto3 client-setup function accepting Config, an explicitly supplied ready AWS-call function, and a supplied outcome-reporting function. Leave retry configuration and ClientError handling incomplete; include prepared outcomes with and without RequestId.
live_code.observable_success: The configured budget permits at most three requests, including the initial request. The application invokes the supplied function once and leaves eligible retries and backoff to the SDK. A successful return is reported as success; a raised ClientError produces failure reporting containing its code and message, plus its request ID when available. Missing RequestId does not cause a new exception.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the supplied-call boundary, standard retry configuration, and ClientError reporting path. Annotate total_max_attempts=3 as one initial request plus at most two retries, contrast Config max_attempts=3 as three retries after the initial request, and identify where Code, Message, and optional RequestId enter the final report.

teaching_notes: Use supplied call and ClientError handling; do not invent error codes, additional retry causes or independent retry loops.

context.concept_name: Identify avoidable charges with Cost Explorer

coverage.learning_objective: Identify avoidable charges with Cost Explorer

required_facts.statement: Cost Explorer analyzes billed cost and usage for selected time intervals and grouping dimensions.
Filter the supplied period and account, group by service or usage type, and inspect the cost and usage values to identify the supported cost driver.
Use the billed usage evidence to justify the avoidable charge rather than equating the existence of a resource with a specific charge.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A resource looks unused, but an avoidable-charge claim needs billed cost and usage evidence. Start with the approved account and time interval, then locate the supported driver in the report.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost Explorer analyzes billed cost and usage for selected time intervals and grouping dimensions.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter the supplied period and account, group by service or usage type, and inspect the cost and usage values to identify the supported cost driver.

Use the billed usage evidence to justify the avoidable charge rather than equating the existence of a resource with a specific charge.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter Cost Explorer to the supplied account and period and group by service or usage type. Compare cost and usage values for the suspected driver. Suppose the supplied report attributes a charge to a particular usage type during that interval: cite those values as the reason for the recommendation. Do not assign a numerical charge to a resource merely because it exists. Keep the filtered period, grouping and report values with the conclusion so that the claim is about observed billed usage. This is identifying a supported cost driver, not estimating future workload cost or independently deciding to delete the resource.

Keep billed cost and usage as the basis for the recommendation, not just the apparent resource age or name. If two suspected drivers exist, compare their report categories in the supplied interval before selecting the one the evidence supports. The recommendation should cite the chosen service or usage-type grouping and its values so a reviewer can reproduce the cost attribution without inventing a charge from a resource inventory.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Resource existence is not evidence of a specific billed charge. Cost Explorer analyzes billed cost and usage; use that evidence to justify the avoidable driver. A suspected idle resource is a lead for inspection, not the entire cost conclusion.

video_need.reason: A short billing filter/group walkthrough helps locate actual usage evidence; text suffices for the evidence-versus-resource distinction.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect one supplied billing dataset using Cost Explorer controls: filter to the supplied account and period, group by service or usage type, and identify an actionable avoidable charge supported by billed cost and usage evidence.
practice_anchor.success: The selected driver matches the filtered billing evidence. The recommendation cites the account, period, service or usage-type grouping, and associated cost and usage values, using supplied context to explain why the charge is avoidable rather than inferring a charge from resource existence. It recommends an action for review without estimating future costs or deleting resources.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the selected account and period, service or usage-type grouping, and corresponding billed cost and usage values visible together so the cost-driver conclusion can be checked against the report.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce price estimates or unapproved teardown; use the supplied billing evidence.

context.concept_name: Operate an EKS Deployment using supplied cluster-access setup

required_facts.statement: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to reconcile the requested Pod replicas and Pod template.
Apply the supplied Deployment with kubectl apply -f FILE and inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and the associated Pods.
Delete one controlled test Pod and verify the controller creates a replacement and restores the requested replica count.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied EKS Deployment requests a fixed number of Pods. The lab removes one Pod to test controller reconciliation, so distinguish the removed Pod's lifecycle from the Deployment's requested state.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to reconcile the requested Pod replicas and Pod template.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied Deployment with kubectl apply -f FILE and inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and the associated Pods.

Delete one controlled test Pod and verify the controller creates a replacement and restores the requested replica count.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Apply the supplied Deployment with kubectl apply -f FILE. Inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and its associated Pods, noting the requested replica count in the exercise. Delete the one approved controlled test Pod through the supplied procedure. Inspect again until the controller creates a replacement and restores the requested count. For an illustrative three-replica workload, the evidence should show the controlled loss and return to the requested three replicas, rather than merely the disappearance of the deleted Pod. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets to reconcile replicas and the Pod template; this exercise does not change load-driven capacity or administer the cluster control plane.

Read requested and observed counts separately during the test. The requested three replicas remain the controller's target; the temporary observed shortage is the controlled condition being reconciled. Completion evidence is the replacement and restored requested count, not the fact that deletion was accepted. Do not describe this task as demand-based scaling, since it preserves a supplied desired count rather than changing it in response to load.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Deleting one test Pod is not changing the Deployment's requested replica count. The controller reconciles the requested Pods and template. Verify replacement and restored count rather than treating the removed Pod's final state as the workload's final state.

video_need.reason: Removing one controlled Pod and observing controller replacement makes desired-replica reconciliation visible over time.

practice_anchor.objective: With cluster access supplied, apply the supplied three-replica Deployment using kubectl apply -f FILE. Inspect kubectl get deployment NAME and the associated Pods through the supplied inspection procedure. Remove one approved test Pod through the supplied deletion procedure, then observe reconciliation.
practice_anchor.success: Evidence records the requested three replicas and associated Pods before deletion, identifies the removed Pod and its replacement, and confirms that the requested count remains three and the observed count returns to three. Deletion acceptance alone does not establish success.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the Deployment's unchanged requested count visible alongside associated Pod identities and observed counts before removal, during reconciliation, and after replacement. Show that a new Pod replaces the removed Pod and restores the requested three replicas.

teaching_notes: Use supplied cluster access and deletion procedure; do not add kubectl commands absent from allowed knowledge.

context.concept_name: Plan infrastructure and data restoration in dependency order

required_facts.statement: A workload recovery plan must account for dependencies and the recovery capabilities needed to satisfy its objectives.
List the supplied infrastructure, data and service dependencies and place each prerequisite restoration before the steps that depend on it.
Include verification points before dependent services resume so incomplete restoration is not mistaken for usable recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A recovery plan can name all components yet still put them in an unusable order. Build the sequence from supplied dependencies and require evidence that each prerequisite is ready before its dependent work resumes.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A workload recovery plan must account for dependencies and the recovery capabilities needed to satisfy its objectives.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
List the supplied infrastructure, data and service dependencies and place each prerequisite restoration before the steps that depend on it.

Include verification points before dependent services resume so incomplete restoration is not mistaken for usable recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose the supplied dependency record says the application needs a restored database and the database needs prepared infrastructure. Put infrastructure restoration before database restoration and database verification before application resumption. These dependencies are example exercise inputs, not a universal AWS recovery sequence. Add the supplied verification point before each dependent service proceeds. If an earlier restoration step is incomplete, the plan should not present its dependent service as ready merely because that later step was scheduled. Compare the complete ordered plan with the stated recovery objectives and capabilities. The useful output is an evidence-checkable dependency order, not an unrelated checklist of resources.

Read each dependency edge as a precondition: a dependent step cannot be considered usable until its prerequisite restoration passes the supplied verification. If independent branches exist in the supplied record, avoid inventing an order between them that the dependencies do not require. The final plan should still make every dependent service's readiness checkpoint explicit and be compared with the stated recovery objectives.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Listing dependencies is not the same as ordering them. Each prerequisite restoration belongs before dependent steps, and verification belongs before dependent services resume. Incomplete restoration must not be treated as usable recovery.

video_need.reason: A dependency graph with readiness checkpoints clarifies why restoration steps must precede dependent services.

practice_anchor.objective: Order the supplied infrastructure restoration, database restoration, verification, and application resumption steps using one workload's supplied dependency record, recovery objectives, and recovery capabilities.
practice_anchor.success: Every prerequisite restoration precedes its dependent step, and every supplied readiness verification precedes dependent service resumption. The plan is compared with the stated recovery objectives and capabilities, without imposing an unsupported order on independent steps.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied infrastructure-to-database-to-application dependencies visible, with readiness verification checkpoints between prerequisite restoration and dependent work. Distinguish any independent branches without implying a universal AWS recovery sequence.

teaching_notes: Use supplied dependency graph and objectives; do not invent a mandatory service-wide recovery ordering.

context.concept_name: Query logs to correlate a service symptom

coverage.learning_objective: Correlate a service symptom using logs

required_facts.statement: Logs Insights queries select and transform log events using commands connected with pipe characters.
Select the log group and time window, then use fields @timestamp, @message, REQUEST_FIELD | filter REQUEST_FIELD = "ID" | sort @timestamp asc with the actual supplied request field and identity.
Use shared request identity and event timestamps to reconstruct the supplied symptom’s sequence, retaining the relevant events as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An orders request failed, and structured logs carry the same request identity across relevant events. Query a bounded time window and reconstruct the supplied sequence from that identity and timestamps rather than from unrelated nearby messages.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Logs Insights queries select and transform log events using commands connected with pipe characters.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Select the log group and time window, then use fields @timestamp, @message, REQUEST_FIELD | filter REQUEST_FIELD = "ID" | sort @timestamp asc with the actual supplied request field and identity.

Use shared request identity and event timestamps to reconstruct the supplied symptom’s sequence, retaining the relevant events as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Select the intended log group and supplied interval. Replace REQUEST_FIELD and ID in the query template with the actual field and request identity from the exercise. The fields command selects timestamp, message and request field; filter keeps the chosen identity; sort orders its events by ascending timestamp. Suppose the matching events show request receipt, a later failure message and a final response record. Retain those events in timestamp order as symptom evidence. That sequence supports correlation of this request; it does not automatically prove every nearby error was its cause. The example uses the stated fields, filter and sort commands without adding aggregation syntax or application tracing.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Time proximity alone does not make two log events part of the same request. Use shared request identity and timestamps together, retain the relevant events, and keep the query scoped to the intended group and time window.

video_need.reason: Querying one request identity and ordering its events benefits from a live structured-log query demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Query one supplied structured log group within the supplied time window, substituting the actual request field and identity into the fields/filter/sort template to reconstruct the seeded orders request failure.
practice_anchor.success: The query returns events for the supplied request identity in ascending timestamp order. The learner retains the relevant receipt, failure and response events and uses them to describe the request sequence without treating unrelated nearby messages as evidence.

live_code.required_skill: Adapt and execute a piped Logs Insights query using fields, filter and sort.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a prepared structured orders log group, a supplied time interval, the actual request-field name and request identity, and the query template fields @timestamp, @message, REQUEST_FIELD | filter REQUEST_FIELD = "ID" | sort @timestamp asc. Include matching receipt, failure and response events alongside unrelated events.
live_code.observable_success: The learner selects the intended group and interval, replaces both placeholders correctly, executes the query, and retains the matching events in ascending timestamp order as evidence for the seeded failure sequence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the selected log group and time interval, the completed fields/filter/sort query, and its timestamp-ordered results visible together so the shared request identity and relevant event sequence can be checked.

teaching_notes: Trace the supplied fields/filter/sort query; do not add untaught query functions or X-Ray tracing.

context.concept_name: Route alarm notifications to an operational owner

coverage.learning_objective: Route alarm notifications to an owner

required_facts.statement: An alarm action can publish state-change notifications to an SNS topic without changing the alarm’s metric evaluation.
Configure the approved topic as the alarm’s notification action and create the approved recipient subscription, confirming it when required.
Verify the recipient receives a test alarm notification containing alarm and workload context; a configured but unconfirmed subscription may not deliver notifications.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm must reach the operational owner, not merely change state. Set up the approved notification route and verify receipt independently of the alarm's metric evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An alarm action can publish state-change notifications to an SNS topic without changing the alarm’s metric evaluation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the approved topic as the alarm’s notification action and create the approved recipient subscription, confirming it when required.

Verify the recipient receives a test alarm notification containing alarm and workload context; a configured but unconfirmed subscription may not deliver notifications.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Configure the approved SNS topic as the alarm action and create the recipient subscription. Confirm it where required. Send the supplied test alarm notification and check that the intended recipient receives alarm and workload context. Retain receipt evidence alongside the subscription configuration. An unconfirmed subscription may not deliver, so configured is not the same as received.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Notification routing does not change the alarm's metric evaluation. A topic action and a recipient subscription need a receipt test; configuration alone, especially an unconfirmed subscription, is not delivery evidence.

video_need.reason: Subscription setup, confirmation where needed and actual notification receipt benefit from a short route verification demonstration.

media.group_title: Connect an alarm to its notification recipient

segments.label: Configure an SNS email notification route and understand subscription confirmation
segments.summary: An SNS topic provides the notification route for an alarm entering ALARM state. The example creates a topic with an email recipient, reviews the configuration, and saves the alarm. Notification actions can also be configured for other states. The alarm initially shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA and later reaches OK. The recipient must accept the email subscription confirmation before receiving notifications; the confirmation step is described rather than demonstrated. The presenter suggests lowering the threshold to test email delivery, but does not demonstrate receipt of a test notification.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the SNS topic connects the alarm to an email recipient. The presenter calls this an “outbound hook.” Use the supplied approved topic, recipient, and test; do not follow the threshold-lowering suggestion.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains subscription confirmation but does not demonstrate contextual test receipt or establish unchanged metric evaluation. The text covers both: preserve evaluation settings and verify the intended owner receives alarm and workload context.

practice_anchor.objective: Connect one supplied CloudWatch alarm to the approved SNS topic and recipient endpoint, confirm the subscription when required, and use the supplied test alarm notification to verify receipt.
practice_anchor.success: The supplied alarm uses the approved SNS topic as its notification action without changes to metric evaluation. The approved recipient subscription is confirmed when required, and receipt evidence shows that the intended operational owner received the supplied test notification containing alarm and workload context.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make visible the supplied alarm's approved SNS notification action, the approved recipient endpoint and subscription confirmation status, and the received test notification containing alarm and workload context.

teaching_notes: Use supplied SNS topic/recipient and test; leave fault injection to its dedicated concept.

context.concept_name: Run a bounded operational action with Lambda

coverage.learning_objective: Run a bounded Lambda operational action

required_facts.statement: A Lambda execution role grants the function permission to access AWS resources during invocation.
Assign the approved execution role whose actions and resources are limited to the supplied operational task.
Invoke the function with the supplied payload and inspect its returned result and execution logs, distinguishing successful invocation from a successful operational result.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied Lambda function performs one bounded operational task. Its execution role must cover that task's approved actions and resources, and invocation evidence must be separated from the operational result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A Lambda execution role grants the function permission to access AWS resources during invocation.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign the approved execution role whose actions and resources are limited to the supplied operational task.

Invoke the function with the supplied payload and inspect its returned result and execution logs, distinguishing successful invocation from a successful operational result.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign the approved execution role scoped to the supplied task. Invoke the function with the supplied payload and inspect both the returned result and execution logs. For an illustrative resource check, suppose the invocation succeeds but the returned task result says the expected operation failed. Preserve that distinction instead of describing the task as successful because the function was invoked. The execution role grants access to AWS resources during invocation; it is not an unlimited operating identity. This exercise evaluates the supplied payload and task result, not independent function-feature development or serverless capacity configuration.

For the opposite case, suppose the supplied function returns a task-success result and the execution logs support that outcome. Record both with the approved payload and role context. That verifies this bounded task execution, not every operation the function could conceivably perform. If the task needs an action absent from the approved role, report the permission/result evidence instead of broadening the role during the test.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Successful invocation is not proof of a successful operational outcome. Read the supplied task result and logs under the approved execution role. Keep the role's bounded actions/resources separate from the mere ability to invoke the function.

video_need.reason: Invocation response, execution logs and the operational task result benefit from observing one bounded function execution.

practice_anchor.objective: Assign the approved scoped execution role to one supplied Lambda operational function, invoke it with the supplied payload, and inspect its returned result and execution logs.
practice_anchor.success: The assigned role permits only the approved task's actions and resources. The supplied payload is used unchanged, and the recorded outcome distinguishes successful invocation from operational success or failure using the returned task result and execution logs, without broadening permissions.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the supplied function's assigned execution role and its bounded actions and resources alongside the supplied invocation payload, returned task result, and execution logs, making invocation status and operational outcome separately visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied function and payload; do not introduce serverless concurrency or application authoring.
